speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The new developments in Poland this past weekend indicate the difficulties of finding long-term solutions in that country. Yesterday, Pope John Paul II asked on behalf of his people that there be no violence. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans):
That this House go on record that there be no outside interference, that Poland be allowed to solve its own problems and that the people of Canada will provide economic assistance to the people of Poland consistent with the needs of the Polish people.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I seek the attention of all hon. members of the House on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Whereas Canadians are greatly concerned over the recent developments in Poland, and whereas Canadians strongly adhere to the principles of the Helsinki Accord with special references to basic human rights and freedoms, and whereas Canadians support the citizens of Poland in the struggle to acquire those basic freedoms to which they have a right, and whereas Pope John Paul II yesterday asked that solutions be arrived at without violence, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle):
That the House urge all nations of the world to refrain from any political or military actions that may in any way interfere with the internal affairs of Poland and that this House express the wish that Poland's internal difficulties will be solved by peaceful negotiations between the Polish government and the Polish people.

speechtext:

speechtext:

subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF CHARTER PROVISIONS TO PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. After an overwhelming majority of members approved the constitutional resolution, which contains a Charter of Rights and Freedoms, this House allegedly followed ancient usage and custom and voted to expel a member for exercising the right to freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression stipulated in the charter without recognizing the rights enunciated in the charter. I move accordingly , seconded by the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson):
That this House demonstrate its real approval of fundamental rights and freedoms by making the provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms apply forthwith to proceedings in the House as part of the Standing Orders so that the charter will govern over these ancient usages and customs that now apply.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister I will direct my question to the Acting Prime Minister. It refers to the events on the weekend in Poland. Has the government made it clear in any official manner to the U.S.S.R. how seriously we would view any interference in Poland by the U.S.S.R.? Has the government made any representations to the Government of Poland deploring the actions taken this weekend, or any representations at all to the Government of Poland? In short, what representations, if any, have been made by the Government of Canada to either the Government of Russia or the Government of Poland?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: POLAND-POSSIBLE INTERVENTION BY U.S.S.R.-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was very happy to hear some of the resolutions in the House today. If some were refused by this

December 14, 1981
Oral Questions
side, or by the other side, it was because of a question of wording and not because of how this government views the Polish situation. With regard to the hon. member's question, the Secretary of State for External Affairs was in Dublin yesterday or the day before, where he publicly stated that Canada is watching the evolving situation in Poland with very keen interests. He appealed to everyone, both inside and outside Poland, to refrain from taking any actions which could jeopardize the situation in Poland. We are of the opinion that the situation in Poland can be resolved in a peaceful manner. We believe that this is possible.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we all know that Canada is watching. The whole world is watching. My question was to the Acting Prime Minister and it is still not answered. Has Canada made any representations in an official way to the U.S.S.R. or the Government of Poland in connection with events this past weekend? If so, what were the representations? We all know that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is watching. We are all watching.
My supplementary question, if the Acting Prime Minister will answer, is this. Are we now in communication with our embassy in Poland? Can we communicate with them? Are we hearing from them? Would either the Acting Prime Minister or the Minister of National Defence make a full statement on motions concerning the Polish situation? Is either minister prepared to make a statement on motions today outlining for us just what is happening and what position Canada is taking?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think it is clear that in the final analysis, this government has always defended the rights and freedoms of nations. When, on earlier occasions, questions have been asked in this House regarding Poland and Afghanistan, the conclusion was always that it was up to the people themselves to decide what their future should be.
Regarding the question of whether we are in touch with our embassy in Warsaw or with other cities, I would say that it is very difficult right now to have any communications with our embassy in Warsaw, for the obvious reason that the borders are closed and communications are controlled by the military and by the present Polish government. However, we remain constantly in touch with the capital cities of NATO member countries, who are also watching the situation very closely. Perhaps the hon. member does not like it when we say that we are watching the situation in Poland with interest, but I think that in reacting to these events, our main concern should be the interests of the Polish people. There could be serious consequences if a country failed to show restraint or did not act wisely.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am asking the minister whether his government, the Government of Canada, has made any official representations to the U.S.S.R., advising of our views with respect to any interference by them in Polish internal affairs, or any representations to the Government of Poland about events on the weekend? Have we made any official representations? We all know the world is watching, and so is Canada. Can the minister answer those questions? Will he make a statement on motions on what the government has done, if anything?
Also, can he tell us is the government satisfied that any Canadian nationals, who are now in Poland, are safe? Is the government satisfied with respect to that? Could the minister just answer these questions, because it is a serious issue that we want some serious answers to, or would the minister like to give us more detail in a statement on motions?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, when I mentioned just now that we were looking very closely at this situation, it should be clear that we are concerned about the situation in Poland and that we are also watching out for the safety of Canadian residents in that country. We have received word that the lives of Canadian residents in Poland are not in danger. The embassy is using all available means to get in touch with them and give them appropriate instructions on what to do until communications are back to normal.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN DISENGAGEMENT OBSERVER FORCE IN MIDDLE EAST
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the same minister, and also deals with the international scene. In view of today's surprising announcement from Tel Aviv, would the Minister of National Defence inform the House what plans Canada has with relation to our troops who are currently participating in UNDOF? What is Canada's official reaction to these events?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN DISENGAGEMENT OBSERVER FORCE IN MIDDLE EAST
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think the reaction of the Canadian troops there today is just the same reaction as they have always had there. We are there as a peacekeeping and information force. I do not think there is any change in that situation as far as our troops are concerned in that part of the world.
December 14, 1981

The minister is surely aware that these are not peacekeeping forces, that they are observers who are unarmed. There are over 200 of them. Will the minister tell the House if he is in any way satisfied that they will be able to perform any useful function, considering the news from Tel Aviv this morning?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, if our 200 people there are observers, who are unarmed, and who are there to examine the situation which is happening in this part of the world, then obviously they are there as a peacekeeping force. They are certainly not aggressive and they are not so conditioned. I can assure the hon. member that if they were not useful to the countries there, they would not be there, because we have a better use for the troops elsewhere.

subsubtopic: DEVELOPMENT OF COPPER MINES IN PERU
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I should like to address my question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. No doubt the minister is aware that over the weekend the Canadian government and some Canadian bankers decided to provide something in the order of $250 million to develop copper mines in Peru. What possible justification is there for spending $250 million Canadian dollars to develop copper mines in Peru when we in Canada have closed one copper mine in Newfoundland, when we are closing one copper mine in British Columbia, and when we are presently laying off in Manitoba where there are two mines that yield a significant amount of copper, thus causing unemployment in Canada, and creating employment with Canadian dollars in another part of the world?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subsubtopic: DEVELOPMENT OF COPPER MINES IN PERU
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the $250 million loan that the hon. member refers to will bring 3,000 person-years of work to Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I would like the minister to enumerate exactly how many Canadians will receive employment as a result of spending $250 million Canadian dollars in Peru, in operations that are, in fact, being closed down in this country, where people are becoming unemployed and where, in fact, we ought to be using those dollars to develop secondary industry here rather than in some other part of the world?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, that is exactly what we are doing. We are employing a great number of Canadians. Goods and machinery will be sourced here in Canada and will provide jobs for Canadians in badly needed areas. I might add that the copper mine that is
Oral Questions
being developed in Peru would have been developed by other sources if it had not been for the aid of Canadians. In this way we are guaranteeing jobs for Canadians. Those mines which are being closed in Canada are being closed for various reasons, including declining ore grade. In this case we are very sure of providing the kind of employment we want for Canadians.
Hear, hear!

Surely the minister recognizes that instead of using Canadian dollars to open up those mines, mines that will pay workers only 86 cents an hour compared to what Canadian workers earn, it would make more sense to use Canadian workers to develop Canadian resources. If we were to do that, we could still put those additional workers to work who will make the machinery. Why are we not using our resource to build our infrastructure in order that we will be in the forefront of world development?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)

Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN LUMBER FREIGHT RATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. In view of the
December 14, 1981

severely depressed state of the lumber industry in northern Ontario as evidenced by mill shutdowns, massive lay-offs, and inventories that are excessively high, I should like to know whether the minister is in a position to use his persuasive powers to prevail upon the Canadian National Railways to postpone for at least a six-month period the very high freight increases for the transportation of lumber that they have announced. These increases will amount to 11 per cent on January 1 and another 5 per cent on June 1. At this time the industry simply cannot bear these costs, which cannot be passed on, and so would mean more lay-offs and higher unemployment in a region that is already suffering too much from these social problems.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN LUMBER FREIGHT RATES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my hon. friend is passing a value judgment under which the railways would be in a better position to foot the bill than the lumber industry would be. speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board. subsubtopic: MR. KING-CALL FOR CESSATION OF NUCLEAR INDUSTRY ACTIVITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the duty to present a petition on behalf of my constituents. The purpose of this petition, which was signed by citizens of the WestBank area in British Columbia and who have formed themselves into an anti-nuclear society named "Candu Won't Do", is to bring to the attention of the House a statement to which 5,903 signatures have been affixed detailing the inherent global hazard to human life itself as a result of slow or catastrophic radiation damage through the use of nuclear technology. The copy page of this statement is attached to this petition.
The nature of the petition is to pray and beseech this House to introduce a bill to Parliament which would stop all nuclear-related activities, including uranium mining, production and sales of Candu reactors and the decommissioning of all existing nuclear reactors.
The petitioners hope, Madam Speaker, that you will find their petition in order and that, through their efforts and this petition, Members of Parliament and the citizens of Canada will be alerted to the magnifying threat to human life posed by nuclear industry activity whether the purpose is for benefit or destruction.

The House resumed, from Friday, November 6, consideration of the motion of (Mr. Caccia) that Bill C-78, an act to provide for the payment of benefits to laid off employees and to amend the Canada Labour Code, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this afternoon we are debating Bill C-78, to provide for the payment of benefits to laid off employees and to amend the Canada Labour Code.
This bill has been with us for a period of time and we are now into second reading. The bill sets out the details of an aid program which is to be made available to older employees who are laid off as a result of plant shutdowns. This program extends benefits now available to certain employees in designated sectors, and this bill is designed to extend these benefits to all industrial sectors. As well, these benefits will extend to community-based programs which were announced jointly by the Departments of Labour, Manpower and Immigration and Industry, Trade and Commerce in the beginning of 1981.
I think it goes without saying that although the bill will provide some worthwhile benefits, it is too little, too late.
There are massive lay-offs occurring at this time, many plants closing and bankruptcies taking place every day. Bankruptcies are up by 50 per cent in small businesses as well as in the farming industry. The budget for this new amendment, I note, is $2.5 million for the fiscal year 1981-82. It will not be retroactive to help all those people who are experiencing great difficulties right now. I think of the Admiral Corporation which laid off 2,400 workers and went into receivership. Those workers are not receiving back pay, holiday pay or benefits that are owing to them. These workers were laid off just before Christmas and they have no relief whatsoever because their benefits are tied up. That is just one example. There are hundreds of other examples throughout Canada which could be cited. Some of my colleagues will be expressing their concerns in this connection later today.
This bill was originally ruled out of order before Parliament adjourned for the summer recess in mid-July. At that time we thought that this bill would go through rather quickly on second reading. However, there are some matters to be discussed before the bill goes to committee later today. It is my understanding that the bill will go through second reading today and into committee tomorrow.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill we are now debating is one which is not launching a massive assault on the problem of unemployment in Canada. It will do nothing for the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are now being laid off as a result of the depression that is now under way because of the incompetent policies of the government which we have had since March, 1980.
Bill C-78 only makes provision for employees of a designated industry which is closed down, and those employees who are laid off will receive certain benefits, if they do not otherwise qualify for benefits. An industry is designated because there has been a significant loss of employment due not to economic recession but to import competition or industrial restructuring or the like. Or an industry is in a region that has been designated by the government. All that is going to happen is that these laid-off employees, as 1 understand it, who are, at least in one category, 54 years of age and have worked in the industry for at least ten of the preceding 15 years, or who were at least 50 years of age, have worked in the industry at least 30 years but are no longer eligible for unemployment insurance, do not qualify for a Quebec or Canada pension and are not able to obtain other work either through job retraining or relocation or both, will receive additional assistance. That is what this bill basically provides for. It is an inadequate response to the present problems we have in this country with respect to unemployment.
It was a pledge of this government in the election of 1979-80 that they were going to do certain things. I just want to put on the record some of the things they said they were going to do. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said this on January 12, 1980:
December 14, 1981

We have an economic program for the eighties which will enhance dignity, create opportunities and provide security.
That was his economic program for the eighties, and we have to ask this government now, where is this program which is going to enhance dignity, create opportunities and provide security? What Canadians have had any security provided for them in the 22 months since this government came to office? What Canadians have had their dignity enhanced by this government's policies since it came to power in February of 1980? What opportunities and what security is being provided? That is what we ask. That was the pledge. Rather than do anything in the economic sphere the Liberals, with the help of the NDP, defeated a government that was doing something along these lines and replaced it. It was on the basis of these promises that they did so.
I want to refer also to a transcript of a press conference the Prime Minister had in Toronto on that day, January 12, 1980. On page 5 of the transcript he was outlining five great principles that were going to be put into effect if they were re-elected. The third one is this:
-we will implement a development and industrial strategy which will provide jobs, spur growth, increase Canadian ownership and control.
Where is it? Where is the growth that has been spurred? We just had a quarter in which the gross national product declined. Where is the industrial strategy that has provided jobs? The only industrial strategy has been to help Massey-Ferguson or Chrysler in their tremendous troubles and to try to save a few jobs there, not to provide additional jobs. Then the statement was made:
This party will not simply stand by and let the recession come. We will fight it and overcome it.
That was the Prime Minister's statement in January of 1980. He was not going to stand by and let the recession come. "We will fight it and overcome it." Where is the fight? Where is the overcoming? Is it represented in this pitiful bill that is now before the House to help a few people if they are over 50 or over age 54 in a designated industry? Is that the great fight against recession? Is the budget of November 12 this great fight against recession? Is the budget of November 12 going to fight and overcome the recession? It is not. It is going to assist the recession, as every observer has said.
The Prime Minister went on to say in the same press conference:
We must increase the economic might of Canada by strengthening each of the regions. We will make the big projects happen, whether they be developing the fishery in the Atlantic, rebuilding the railways in the West, developing new manufacturing strength in Ontario and Quebec, or expanding British Columbia's resource and trade potential. We need a national government that builds up rather than tears down.
How much of that pledge has been carried out? What regions have they strengthened? What region of Canada has been strengthened by this government since it got into this House? I can assure you this: it has weakened the Atlantic region, it has weakened the province of Newfoundland, it has engaged in a dastardly conspiracy and combination to put down the province of Newfoundland because the government of the province of Newfoundland will not bow and will not

accept the dictates of this government. It had a chance in Newfoundland to assist in the field of economic development on a project in my own district, which I will mention briefly just once again, the project of providing a synchrolift for the federally-owned dockyard in St. John's, Newfoundland. It had a chance to assist in the dockyard that it owned that has a great chance for the future. It has been in operation now since the late 1880s. It was given to the Government of Canada as a gift in 1949 when we entered Confederation. This government made a pledge in 1978 to provide the financing for a synchrolift, a three-berth synchrolift, to enable that dockyard to continue to function and be successful in the future; to preserve the 350 jobs that were there and to increase that number by another 150 jobs. Yet rather than carrying that pledge out, and rather than spending the money provided by the PC government in the estimates to start that process of a synchrolift in the federal dockyard in St. John's, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) used the money for some other purpose and cancelled federal assistance for the federally owned dockyard in St. John's, Newfoundland, to provide the synchrolift. They left it to the province, and on Tuesday of last week, December 8, the government of Newfoundland announced a $30 million project at the federal dockyard in St. John's. The financing is to be made available by the province, $10 million in loans and subsidized interest, so that the CN, which operates that dockyard on behalf of the Government of Canada, would go ahead and award the contracts for the synchrolift project.
This is the government that promised to increase the economic might of Canada by strengthening each of the regions. It has deliberately attempted to damage the Newfoundland region because it does not agree with the policies or the statements of the government of the province of Newfoundland and has forced the government of Newfoundland, which is the least able to afford it, to spend money on a federally owned dockyard in St. John's so that that dockyard will be able to persevere in the future, so the 350 jobs that are now there would be saved and another 150 jobs would be created. If that is not the most shameful piece of economic poltroonery ever undertaken by a Government of Canada, I do not know what is. There could not be a worse example than this low, foul, political act of a government that was elected on the basis that they were going to increase the economic might of Canada by strengthening each of the regions.

I can go ahead and give further instances in a few minutes.
At the Toronto press conference the Prime Minister was not Prime Minister then. He was a lot more humble then. He was not the arrogant figure we have seen in the House these last few months with his fascination for the Constitution. Nero fiddles while Canada burns. He is fixated on the Constitution, constipated on the Constitution. There has been no other movement of the government except constitutional movements, and let the economy go. This was his fifth point:

How? He did not say how. Further on he said:
We must endorse the right of every Canadian to have a job.
That was the pledge of the Prime Minister in that campaign, "We must endorse the right of every Canadian to have a job". What is the reality today? You can pick up the paper at any time, Mr. Speaker, and see what the reality is. For the week ending November 4, there were 979,000 people unemployed, an unemployment rate of 8.2 per cent over all nationally. In Newfoundland, my own province, there was an unemployment rate of 15.3 per cent. That is the official rate. In actual fact, it is somewhere between 25 and 30 per cent of the working population of Newfoundland that is unemployed.
Statistics Canada admits that there are 348,000 hidden unemployed in Canada not shown in the figures because they have given up looking for work. There have been no jobs so they are no longer looking for work. Newfoundland is the worst province for that. The participation rate declined last month. There were 50,000 people who dropped out of the labour force. If they had stayed in, the adjusted rate would have been 8.6 per cent. The actual number of people out of work according to the November 4 statistics was 928,000.
Does the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), who just brought down his budget, show any hope for the future? He does not. He forecasts for this year an average unemployment rate of 7.2 per cent. He forecasts for next year, after his tremendous budget is implemented, if it ever is, a rate of 7.8 per cent and in 1983 a rate for the year of 8.3 per cent.
In the last three months, we have been told by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, more than 140,000 workers lost their jobs in Canadian factories, according to Mr. Roy Phillips. It is going to be a long, cold winter, said the spokesman for 8,000 manufacturers. The Ontario labour ministry says 67 plants in the province, 34 of them in the Toronto area, have already shut down. Another 89 have curtailed operations. On and on it goes.
The worst situation of all with reference to employment is in Newfoundland. This government, rather than attempting to help Newfoundlanders and the Newfoundland government overcome this tremendous problem of unemployment, has deliberately acted to decrease employment in Newfoundland by withdrawing federal assistance from a federal project, a federally-owned dockyward in St. John's and by refusing to enter into DREE agreements. It has refused to sign an agreement and spend transportation moneys in Newfoundland. It is now engaged in cutting off or reducing ferry service from North Sydney to Argentia. One of the two ferries will be taken off next year. It is going to reduce employment in the Argentia area of Newfoundland, one of the worst hit areas already with respect to employment in the whole island of Newfoundland. That is the Prime Minister's program when in office.
Let us look again at the hypocrisy. This is the most hypocritical and pusillanimous government this country has ever had and, in my book, the Prime Minister is the most reprehensible. This is what the Prime Minister said, and I quote from the Toronto Star of April 24, 1980:
-it's more important to create jobs and ensure economic growth than to reduce the federal deficit.
He has not passed that message on to Mr. MacEachen. I quote his exact words:
"We're not obsessed by the deficit in the same way as Mr. Clark's government was," Trudeau said at his weekly news conference yesterday.
"We will not reduce the deficit at the expense of creating more unemployment."

Mr. Speaker, I should like to examine the contents of Bill C-78, which is an act to provide for the payment of benefits to laid off employees and to amend the Canada Labour Code. That sounds innocent enough until one examines the bill. The government wants to set up a labour adjustment benefits board; it wants to adjust policies and programs that it has not had the initiative to correct before this. It wants to bring in a band-aid bill to help provide some relief.
Let us examine the limited relief that this bill would provide, Mr. Speaker. In order to qualify for relief, an area would have to be designated. A qualified employee would have to be a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident of this country between 54 and 65 years of age or between 50 and 54 with 30 years' service in the industry. He would have to have been employed for ten years out of the past 15 in a designated industry. He would have to have been laid off in an action affecting 10 per cent of the work force or 50 employees. Imagine how many people those provisions will help when 140,000 people in the manufacturing industry have been laid off in the last three months.
In his opening remarks the minister indicated that the Canadian Labour Congress is sympathetic to the bill. I should like to put on record some recommendations offered by the Canadian Labour Congress. They are as follows:
One year advance notice of plant closures and major lay-offs and six months for lay-offs of less than 50 employees.
That sounds reasonable enough.
Further recommendations are:
All lay-offs must be justified in hearings before a Job Protection Board.
Before lay-offs take place, the employer must consult with the union on ways to avoid job loss; if lay-offs cannot be prevented, an agreement must be reached with the union covering the terms of the lay-off.
Standard hours of work must be lowered through collective bargaining; all overtime work must be voluntary; overtime pay must be increased to two and a half times the regular rate.
These are constructive proposals, Mr. Speaker. At various times in this House I have put forward a program regarding the railway industry. This government has not seen fit to bring in legislation covering the working hours of employees; consequently, they are being forced to work as much as 11 hours while at the same time lay-offs are taking place all across Canada. I think that is a shame. The government should look at areas where job opportunities exist and not force people to

December 14, 1981
Labour Adjustment Benefits
work up to 11 hours in the operating trades of the railway industry. The next recommendation is:
Severance pay of one week per year of service.
Is that too much to ask for an employee being laid off? Other recommendations follow:
Relocation allowances to be paid by the employer in case of lay-offs. Compensation payments to the community affected by lay-offs may be paid out of a special fund into which employers contribute.
I think this is a very important point which has never been examined. When lay-offs occur in small communities it becomes a local disaster, and those communities have difficulty in maintaining their schools, recreation facilities and the normal services that they provide. This bill still only proposes to designate a few employees and leave the others to try to maintain themselves and their communities. That is wrong, Mr. Speaker, and the Minister of Labour must identify those areas. The next recommendation is as follows:
A grant-levy system to ensure that all employers contribute to the cost of retraining workers.
I think that is an excellent proposal and it should not be too hard to reach agreement on it. The final recommendation is:
Changes in pension legislation to improve vesting rights and ensure portability of pensions.
These are the recommendations of the CLC to the Minister of Labour, Mr. Speaker, so I think he was wrong in his opening remarks when he said that the Canadian Labour Congress was basically in sympathy with the bill being presented.
We in this party are skeptical about the bill, Mr. Speaker. We believe that there are serious problems with lay-offs. The Minister of Labour should bring in legislation to retrain people and to find ways of keeping employment going. The lumber industry in British Columbia is a prime example of where this is needed. That industry is staggering, the country is in need of housing, but the Minister of Labour appears to want to designate such areas as ones that may qualify for some adjustment assistance.
How would it come about, if someone were to be able to get under those kinds of programs? If it were a designated area, and if someone were trying to participate in the program, he would want to use the rules of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. If the commission were in doubt, it would put the member before a board of referees. We all know about these boards of referees. It is a great system! A board has an employee representative and a commission representative sitting on it, and a chairman is selected. It sounds like a reasonable approach and one which should work. However, time after time we have seen a board of referees hand down a unanimous decision that someone qualifies for benefits, but the commission has made that person go to an independent umpire, one person sitting and making judgment and, nine times out of ten, the judgment is in favour of the commission. That is the way the commission wants to conduct the appeal
procedure when there is something in doubt. I think that is wrong and this portion of the bill must be corrected.
A portion of the bill increases the notice period of lay-off to 16 weeks from the current eight weeks and makes a shift adjustment in severance benefits to a maximum of five days. Again, it is weak and it is not sufficient. It needs many changes.
We in this party are opposed to Bill C-78. We will be fighting against it in committee. We will be asking witnesses to come forward to present their concerns. In fact, we will be trying to improve the bill and to bring about some other recommendations which we think can help bring about some programs which will be acceptable and will meet the needs of all people who are laid off, not only the very few. Hopefully the government, in its wisdom, will also bring about a bill to include training and other aspects under this program which will help find other areas in which people can relocate. We think it is very important that the government move very swiftly to bring about needed changes, instead of this band-aid approach which it has put before us here today.

However, if Your Honour would excuse me, there are some things I would like to speak about dealing with the Canada Labour Code, which is one of the matters contained in the bill before us. There are basically two parts to this bill, one dealing with labour adjustment benefits and the second dealing with amendments to the Canada Labour Code. However, first of all, because on occasion I tend to speak for too long and am not able to say everything I would like to say, I want to address myself to some omissions in this bill, some amendments which might be made to the Canada Labour Code but which are not included in this bill. I refer to amendments which might prove very beneficial to the Northwest Territories concerning matters which my constituents and people in other parts of the Northwest Territories have tried to accomplish for very many years.
The Canada Labour Code is divided into various parts which deal with different aspects of labour law. For instance, Part III deals with labour standards. As matters rest at present, the Northwest Territories is treated in the same manner as any other jurisdiction in Canada. They are able to pass their own labour standards legislation. In fact, they have done a pretty good job with this. We have heard very little complaint concerning labour standards in that area of the country. It is good that we should be able to do this, because some of the conditions of labour in remote areas of Canada and northern Canada are quite different from those which exist, say, in the metropolitan areas of Toronto or Quebec.
December 14, 1981

People are engaged in different types of activity and there is need for a different way of approaching labour problems.
One of the things we tend to find in that part of the world is that people come into a certain area for several weeks and work long hours because there is nothing else to do with their time off, and then they take the next two or three weeks off in their home communities. Under our labour standards ordinance, that type of activity is allowed.
Part IV of the Canada Labour Code deals with safety legislation. Again, the territories enact and enforce their own safety ordinances. I am pleased to acknowledge the fact that, within the last few months, the territorial government has taken over the administration of the mining safety ordinances. For a long time this has been territorial legislation, but its administration was in federal hands. It is a step in the right direction that the territories have now taken over that aspect of administration.
However, we now come to Part V of the Canada Labour Code. As all hon. members of this House are aware, Part V deals with labour relations. It deals with conciliation, with mediation, with certification of unions and all these types of things. Under Section 108 of Part V of the Canada Labour Code, this part is not treated the same in the territories as the other parts. The territorial authorities are prevented from enacting their own legislation dealing with mediation, conciliation, certification of unions and all these types of things which, in a province, are done by the provincial government. For many years, there has been a feeling, for two reasons, that we should proceed with amendments to the Canada Labour Code to allow the territories to take over that area of jurisdiction. I am sure that, in the first place, the reason they were not allowed the same rights as other provinces was largely an oversight.
There are two reasons, and the first is really political. Everyone knows that the territories aspire to provincial status. It is a step in the right direction to take on these additional responsibilities. Judging from the manner in which they have conducted their affairs under Part III and Part IV of the Canada Labour Code, it seems quite reasonable to suppose that they would do an equally good job under Part V.
The second reason is a more practical reason. The people who work for Labour Canada, such as conciliators, mediators and everyone else, generally do a pretty good job. We are fortunate in this country to have good government employees doing those jobs. However, they are always concerned with the great national issues. If there is a strike in Vancouver harbour, they will obviously be very concerned with that and try to get it resolved. If there are problems on the railways-and there are likely to be many more with the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin)-they will be concerned with that. A strike of garbage workers in a small municipality in the Northwest Territories or a strike in a small mine which does not really affect the whole affairs of the nation will not receive the attention that it deserves. Such a strike is remote, it is out of the way, it is not a great national problem, and it will always be put in second place. The same is true when it comes
Labour Adjustment Benefits
to certification of unions. There are always hundreds of thousands of employees with federal undertakings which must be looked after in the south, while 50 members of a local union somewhere in the north just do not really count for that much in the general scheme of things. It would be good for practical reasons to have this take place.
The idea of this transfer of authority receives the support of practically everyone in the territories. It was supported by the seventh legislature of the territories, by the eighth legislature and now by the ninth. Various legislatures over a period of 15 years have continued to ask for this, and I hope they will achieve these goals in short order. The move certainly has the support of the labour unions in the Northwest Territories, and as far as I know it has the support of employer organizations. I have heard members of chambers of commerce speaking in favour of that move.
In fact, I have with me here today a letter I received from Mr. Christopher Reid, president of the Northwest Territories Teachers' Association. He addresses himself to this very issue and suggests that the problem could easily be rectified by amending offending Section 108 of Part V of the Canada Labour Code, and he suggests the following wording:
This part applies in respect of employees who are employed upon or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business, other than a work, undertaking or business of a local or private nature in the Northwest Territories, and in respect of the employers of all such employees in their relations with such employees, and in respect of trade unions and employers' organizations composed of such employees or employers.
I think that is an excellent suggestion.
You are probably aware, Mr. Speaker, of a rather famous case that occurred a few years ago when there were some labour problems in a municipality in the territories, in the city of Yellowknife. If you read existing Section 108 you might, had it not been for the court ruling, have interpreted it to allow the territories to enact their own legislation. As a result of that case, where a municipality was found to be a federal undertaking in the territories that interpretation was cut out. It is now necessary to amend the Canada Labour Code. The process for doing this would be fairly easy.
There should be negotiations between the Government of Canada and the government of the territories. The territories should bring in their own legislation governing certification of unions, etc., and the amendment to the Canada Labour Code should be made by this House. They could both then come into force as of the same day so there would be no period when workers would not be covered in that area of jurisdiction. That is my submission with respect to Part V of the Canada Labour Code.

If you are talking to someone who will be laid off from one of the designated industries, the first thing he will ask is, "How much will I get out of this?" When discussing this with the Canadian taxpayer who will foot the bill, the first thing he will ask about the bill is, "How much will it cost? How much will I be paying the person who is laid off? I do not mind helping out a little, but how much will it cost?"
When I study this bill, I find that the very basic and fundamental piece of information which people want to know about is not there. The very thing that people are most concerned about in this type of bill does not appear in it. It does not indicate how much a laid-off worker will be eligible to receive. It is to be computed by one of these long, Liberal formulae made up of all sorts of calculus and algebra, computed on the basis of all kinds of rules and regulations which have yet to be made.
My next concern which I feel should be dealt with at length in committee is that this bill will create two classes of unemployed. First, there will be those people who are over 54 who have been laid off but are fortunate enough to be from a designated industry. Not all individuals will be treated the same.
There are many rules and regulations which must be met in order for an industry to be designated as certifiable or not. Those who are laid off from a designated industry will be fortunate as opposed to an individual who is out of work but is not eligible because he was laid off from a different type of industry. An illustration of this would be to consider two individuals aged 55, one working in a shoe factory and the other in a sawmill. Because the Liberals have put mortgage
Labour Adjustment Benefits
interest rates too high, no one can afford to build a house and the person working in the sawmill is laid off. He does not have any money and does not know where his next meal will come from. On the other hand, the government may change the tariff quotas, thus putting the person working in the shoe factory out of work. But in all probability the shoe factory will be designated as a certifiable industry and that worker will be eligible for all those benefits-even though we do not know what they are. The unemployed sawmill worker will not receive a nickel.
I believe this may lead to all sorts of discrimination and other actions which are not in the best interests of Canadian unity. If you are the shoe factory worker-which a lot of Liberals should be-and you see this industry failing, you know that in a couple of years you will be looked after by the government. Therefore, there is no incentive to seek retraining or perhaps to go to Alberta to get a job on an oil rig which is going to the United States anyway. It is more advantageous to stay put and wait for a government handout while everything goes down the drain. This is a built-in inequity and an incentive for inefficiency.
Of particular interest to me and to people in my constituency are those who find themselves in the same position as those contemplated in this bill. There are many people aged between 55 and 65 years old who, through no fault of their own, have been left aside by the modern world. They are people who were born into a tradition of hunting, trapping and living off the land. The wage economy in the modern world has caught up with them and passed them by. Many of these people really have nothing to look forward to. They do not speak English and it is very difficult to learn in later life. They do not really have any marketable skills and there is nothing for them to look forward to until they are eligible for the old age pension. To me, it would seem very unjust if people in Montreal and Quebec City who worked in the textile mills and shoe factories were looked after at government expense, providing early retirement for them while the people in my constituency, for whom I have a great deal of concern and much appreciation of their difficulties, are not looked after. They are once again in a position where they have been cast aside and the government is taking no particular interest in them. It is tantamount to telling some Canadians that they are expendable. I hope this problem will be resolved when this bill goes to committee.
I believe it must be realized that once legislation of this sort has been passed, there will always be pressure to expand it. An example of this is DREE. This program was introduced in a few small areas of high unemployment and people in adjacent areas want to have it expanded. Then somebody else put up a good case, so we end up now with a system whereby DREE operates virtually Canada-wide.
We will have to be somewhat careful about the pressures which will be put on the government to expand this program, if it is ever put into effect. It will only be natural for unions to push for the same provisions to be applied not only in initially

designated regions but also, eventually, across the country. With respect to the 54-year limit, we can expect pressure to be applied to reduce that to perhaps 50 years or even 45 years. That is something about which we will have to be pretty careful when we are looking at the labour adjustment benefit provisions in this bill.
I will say just a few words about the second part of Bill C-78, which deals with amendments to the Canada Labour Code. I spoke earlier on in my presentation, about amendments I would like to have seen and now I will say just a few words about the amendments contained in the bill. The first one deals with notice of termination. At the present time, as I understand it, if an employer has 100 employees, he has to give eight weeks' notice. If he has 100 to 300 employees, he must give 12 weeks' notice. If he has over 300 employees, he must give 16 weeks' notice. Under the new provisions, 16 weeks' notice of termination is required of all employers if they intend to lay off 50 or more workers within a period of, I think, four weeks. My initial reaction to this is that I think soon we will see numerous blocks of 49 workers at a time being laid off from various industrial concerns. However, whatever figure we choose, I suppose there will be that problem.
I listened carefully this afternoon to the submission made by the New Democratic Party. New Democrats always have at heart the concerns of employees, particularly those represented by labour unions. It is my submission that perhaps members of the New Democratic Party go just a little too far. The more difficult we make it for employers, the less likely they are to start up plants or make new investments because they know that if they have to terminate, they have to go through this very expensive process or the process suggested by members of the New Democratic Party. If we make termination requirements too tough, perhaps we will not be doing employees a favour. We will not be doing labour a favour because by decreasing employment opportunities over all we will be making it much more difficult for workers to get jobs in the first place. That is the way the economic system works. I know some members of the New Democratic Party think we can solve all problems by legislation, but we cannot suspend or annul the laws of supply and demand in the long run, and the laws of supply and demand relate to labour in the same way as they do to goods and commodities. That is a caveat I place on some of the remarks made by representatives of the New Democratic Party.
I like the idea of joint planning committees contained in the bill. When an industry is terminated because it can no longer continue and when people have to be laid off, in my opinion it is a good idea if representatives of both the employees and the employer get together and try to work out a system under which terminations can be made the least disruptive as possible and carried out in an orderly manner. I have some reservations about formal legislation dealing with this matter. It would be nice if we could think that by mutual consent employees and employers could enter into such arrangements, but when we pass very specific legislation governing this, we
might on occasion be creating more difficulties than we are solving.
After reading through the provisions of the bill relating to joint planning committees some questions came to my mind. What powers under law would the joint planning committees have? That question is not really addressed in the bill. I would like to refer to Clause 32. The amended Canada Labour Code would read as follows:
60.15 On completion of the development of an adjustment program, the employer shall implement the program and the joint planning committee and any trade union or redundant employees who appointed the members of the committee shall co-operate with and assist the employer in implementing the program.
This gives some authority to the recommendations of the joint planning committee, but it is not at all specific. If the committee makes certain recommendations, there is nothing in the act which says upon whom they should be binding, how they are to be enforced-if, indeed, they are to be enforced- or if they are just recommendations. Proposed Section 60.15 suggests that there is something more than just recommendations. I think that item should be discussed in the committee so that we can find out exactly what should be the powers of a joint planning committee.
These, then, are my observations and recommendations with respect to Bill C-78. As I have said, we support its general concept but we have certain reservations about it. We feel the bill deserves careful consideration in the committee and is capable of considerable improvement. We hope the government will not only proceed with these stop-gap measures but will also make a real effort to promote growth in the economy and to get things going again in this country.
Of particular interest to me and to my constituents in the Northwest Territories-and I have brought this to the attention of Parliament before in respect to desperately needed amendments to the Canada Labour Code-is that the code presently excludes the Northwest Territories from enacting certain types of legislation. I thank Your Honour, and I thank hon. members of the House for their indulgence.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) has just said, our party supports the principle of this bill. We think improvements can be made to the bill, and we look forward to making some of them in the committee.
What we are talking about here is like putting a patch on a tire. We think there should be a new patch on the tire, but the fact that the motor of the car is not working, the body is falling apart and the windows are shattered seems to be irrelevant. All of us are in favour of putting a new patch on a tire when it is not working properly, but-and I hope to get into this in a few moments-this bill is completely oblivious to some of the bigger issues.
I think somebody said earlier that this bill is like trying to put a bit of sand into a hole in a dyke when water is running over the top, around the dyke and through crevices. Here we are, 282 Members of Parliament, focusing on whether we should put a little bit of sand in the dyke. This bit of sand, I
December 14, 1981

am told, amounts to between $2 million and $2.5 million for the fiscal year 1981-82. The government's budget this year will be of the order of $76 billion, and here we are seriously discussing a bill which talks about spending $2.5 million. Considering our industrial and economic problems, this is bizarre and hypocritical and, in the larger scheme of things, an absolute waste of the time of the members of this House.
The bill should have been passed years ago. We should have long ago gone on to the more basic problem of trying to get the Canadian economy working again. I have here The Globe and Mail report on business. By coincidence, it is today's issue. There is a feature on Japan. One whole section is devoted to what the Japanese economy is doing right and, by implication, what the Canadian economy is doing wrong. On the third page there is an article entitled: "Hard work, labour peace help produce the miracle".

They are worried about their labour force working when they are too old. In Canada, we are trying to bring in a measure to assist those who lose their jobs because of our policy of deindustrialization in Canada, which the Liberals cram down the throats of Canadians wanting to work. We end up with measures like the one we are discussing. I quote from that article:
When asked to outline the key features of their labour-management system, Japanese businessmen usually mention several: the enterprise union concept; the lifetime employment system, and consensus decision-making. All three go together.
Why we cannot have some of these concepts in Canada is beyond me. We should have had them 15 years ago. A few pages later is an article headed: "Japanese system feels strain of changing work force", and I quote:
The Japanese work force is shrinking and the age of the Japanese worker is increasing, a trend that has Japanese companies worried.
That is hardly a problem we have to worry about in Canada with the way our economy is managed. On the next page is an article headlined: "Export curbs put brakes on Japanese auto production". It deals with some of the problems in the Japanese auto industry, which I do not have to tell hon. members is virtually flooding the Canadian market.
To digress for a moment, I am told that a substantial number of Lada cars are now being sold in Canada. These cars
Labour Adjustment Benefits
are manufactured in the Soviet Union. I believe they market for about $5,000 each. My information is that that represents approximately a full year's salary for the average Russian. That is the minimum. Those people across the way who are allowing the Lada cars to flood our market could be questioned under GATT as to whether that is an artificially low price. At the same time those opposite bring in a measure to help people who will lose their jobs in the auto industry in Canada with a type of retraining.
On another page we find an article entitled: "Japan's industrial success spurred by selective R and D". I quote:
"Research makes the difference," says the motto on shopping bags with the Sony label. It is an aphorism that helps account for the great leap forward not only at Sony Corp., rebounding from a slump that depressed sales and profits in the 1970s, but also at other high technology industries.
I need not say that R and D in Canada is desperately inferior by comparison. After passing this bill, we could spend our time seeing what we can do to encourage R and D. Further on is another article entitled: "Long term economic health tied to handling of surplus". 1 quote:
The Japanese economy will pick up in 1982 after a relatively sluggish performance this year, leading Japanese economists say. But its long-term health may depend on the country's ability to correct-without damage to itself-an enormous surplus on trade with the United States and Europe.
That is an economy dealing with its problems, dealing with them well and benefiting its people accordingly. I could go on. Suffice it to say that this one issue of the paper talks primarily about what the Japanese economy is doing well. There is an interesting chart in this paper which mentions what Canada imports from the Japanese and vice versa. I think it is fair to say that we export such things as meat, wheat, raw materials of various sorts and coal. In turn, we import from the Japanese products such as fabricated materials, steel, iron, cars, auto parts, telecommunications material, film, plates and that sort of thing.
One does not have to take a course in economics to know that if you want people to work after the age of 50 or under the age of 20, you are better to encourage those things which have a high technology and high labour side to them. This is an almost classical example, with Canadians exporting coal and the Japanese shipping back to us all manner of automobiles.
What are we doing in this bill? We are trying to help those who lose their job because of competition from Japan and other economies. We are trying to re-train them to cut fish, dig coal, cut trees or other things for which most are obviously not suited. I suggest we have the whole thing backwards. Similar to Lewis Caroll's "Alice in Wonderland", we are a bunch of serious people considering how to help those who are laid off, instead of considering measures that will get people working, the young, old and middle-aged.
There is no point repeating the arguments made by my colleagues. Obviously we are in favour of an aid program for mature employees who have been laid off as a result of plant shut-downs. Which Member of Parliament could oppose something that will help people in their fifties or early sixties who

have lost their job to be retrained and receive some benefits? Many of these people have given a lifetime of work to a particular firm or occupation. One would have to be a sadist to not want to help such people. I might mention in passing that it is a pity that many of the affected groups such as the Canadian Labour Congress, the various firms and employee associations were not consulted before the bill was presented to us. I hope they will have an opportunity in committee.
Let me refer for a moment to the unemployment situation in Canada. Our unemployment rate is in excess of 8 per cent. I forget exactly how much in excess. Most would agree there are roughly a million Canadians actively looking for work today. As we know, many of these people are young. However, there are many in their thirties, forties and fifties. It is an absolute tragedy that the government is actively encouraging higher and higher rates of unemployment in Canada. I recall a week or so ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) saying that we cannot worry about the rate of unemployment going higher, that we have to go on fighting inflation. The minister has introduced a budget which does nothing but encourage inflation.
I think I just mentioned that the hardest hit group of people unemployed is those between the ages of 15 and 24. As mentioned before, the number of jobs in Ontario decreased by, I believe it was, 140,000 in the month preceding December 9. From an employment standpoint, the situation in many parts of Canada, though not in Alberta, is absolutely critical. I have the figures in front of me but I will keep them out of your sight, Mr. Speaker. They were recently published by the OECD. They refer to the 24 countries that are members of OECD. For instance, in the area of industrial production for Canada, the tip of the graph for the year 1981 points virtually straight down, compared to that of the United States and that of Japan-Austria is bad-Finland, Norway, Belgium and even the United Kingdom.
When we turn to unemployment, we see that the situation in Canada-and again I am comparing the trends in the charts- is bad compared to that in the United States, Australia, Belgium, Austria, Finland, West Germany, Ireland, Holland, Norway, Sweden and even the United Kingdom. I should add that these figures appear to be approximately four months old.
Looking at total trade-and I am doing this just by a test of the eye-on a trend basis, Canada is bad compared to the United States, Japan, Australia, Sweden, France, Italy, Holland and Germany. And so on it goes. Canada is bad compared to virtually every industrialized country, at least in the OECD, whether one looks at agriculture, manufacturing or exports. It is self-evident that the Canadian economy is performing as badly as that of any country in the western advanced industrial world.
Given that fact, one might think-and I think everyone in the Chamber and every Canadian knows-maybe we would be trying to do something to find out why things are working in a country such as West Germany, Japan or many others. Why
are things going so badly in Canada? Not a chance. We are here discussing a bill to help people by grants or retraining who are laid off. The reason the economy is as bad as it is is completely ignored. At a time like this, what do we do? Three weeks ago we introduced a budget which creates nothing but disaster for every conceivable sphere in the Canadian economy except the Canadian Bankers' Association and the Business Council on National Issues. Mr. Speaker, if you can tell me one other group in Canadian society that has one good word to say about the budget, then I would like to know its name.

People are taking their savings and pensions out of the country. They are selling their homes here to buy homes in Arizona or some such place. This party believes in policies and measures designed to attract foreign capital, not policies that will discourage it at every turn. This party believes in policies which would attract more people into Canada with the skills and the training that would be of benefit to the economy, causing it to grow.
Let us take Jamaica as an example, Mr. Speaker. For eight or nine years Michael Manley used the same kind of policies there as this government has been using. He managed to take a perfectly healthy, prospering and relatively happy economy and country to the point where it had an inflation rate of 35 per cent and an unemployment rate of 35 per cent per annum. He drove foreign investment out of Jamaica with his own brand of xenophobia, of which we have not a little in this country, unfortunately. He drove people out of the country and ended up with an unemployment rate of 35 per cent and an

inflation rate of 35 per cent. Eventually the majority of the people of Jamaica had the sense to throw him out of office.
At the weekend I read in the newspaper that Mr. Seaga has brought the inflation rate down to 6 per cent, but I do not know what the unemployment rate is although I believe it has been substantially reduced. Mr. Seaga spoke of attracting investment from 800 businesses which had expressed interest in investing in his country, so money and investment are flooding back to the island. I have never been to Jamaica but I understand it is a magnificent place. When money comes back, jobs come back and with proper control, inflation goes down. If all the things that would encourage inflation were listed, it would be seen that this government has done most of them. If all the things that would encourage unemployment were listed, it would be seen that this government has done most of them too. If a list were made of everything that would drive Canadian money out of the country, it would be seen that this government has done most of them. It is dreadfully wrong for a country with the talents, resources and education we have to try to disembowel itself, economically speaking, year after year after year.
A concrete example of this has occurred in my own community in Alberta, Mr. Speaker. A company there has become the largest producer of rigs for the oil industry throughout the world in the last ten years.
